summary: Specifies version 4 of the Network File System protocol, which lets computers use files stored on remote servers as if they were local. Unlike earlier versions, it integrates file locking and replaces the separate MOUNT protocol. It builds on NFS versions 2 and 3.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to open files stored on another computer as if they were on your own, with built-in rules so two people do not scribble on the same page at once.

questions: what is a compound request in nfsv4
subtitle: The fourth version of NFS: remote files with built-in locking, strong security, batched requests and client caching.

tldr.problem: Earlier NFS versions needed a separate MOUNT protocol and a separate lock manager, had only weak machine-based security, and did not cope well with high-latency, firewalled Internet links.
tldr.mechanism: NFSv4 folds mounting and byte-range locking into one stateful protocol on a single well-known port. It bundles many operations into one COMPOUND request, requires Kerberos V5 security through RPCSEC_GSS, and lets servers hand out recallable delegations so clients can cache aggressively.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7530 replaces RFC 3530 as the definition of NFSv4 minor version 0 without changing what was valid on the wire. It has since been updated by RFC 7931 and RFC 8587.

today: RFC 7530 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3530 as the definition of NFSv4 minor version 0, and it has been updated by RFC 7931 and RFC 8587. It has not itself been obsoleted according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Goals and Lineage of NFSv4
sections.content:
RFC 7530 defines NFS version 4 (NFSv4), the next revision after NFS versions 2 (RFC 1094) and 3 (RFC 1813). It keeps what made the older versions work: easy recovery, independence from transport protocols, operating systems and file systems, simplicity, and good performance.

The stated goals are improved access and performance on the Internet (easy firewall traversal, good behaviour where latency is high and bandwidth is low, and scaling to very large numbers of clients per server), strong security with negotiation built into the protocol, good cross-platform interoperability, and a design that accepts standard extensions without breaking backward compatibility.

This document, together with the companion XDR description in RFC 7531, obsoletes RFC 3530. It introduces no over-the-wire changes, in the sense that previously valid requests remain valid. Where the two documents disagree, RFC 7531 is authoritative for the XDR definitions.

Against RFC 3530 the main changes are a restructured explanation of multi-server namespaces, updated handling of domain names, removal of the previously required LIPKEY and SPKM-3 security mechanisms, and a strengthened definition of the stateid.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a library where you can borrow books from far away. NFS version 4 is the newest set of library rules, made to work well over the big Internet and to keep everyone's borrowing safe.

sections.title: COMPOUND: Many Operations in One Request
sections.content:
NFSv4 has only two RPC procedures: NULL and COMPOUND. Everything else is an operation carried inside COMPOUND, such as LOOKUP, OPEN, READ or WRITE. A request is a tag, a minorversion and an array of operations, and the server evaluates them in order.

This saves round trips. Without any earlier contact with a server, a client can read data from a file in one request by combining LOOKUP, OPEN and READ in a single COMPOUND. The operations share context through a current filehandle and a saved filehandle: PUTFH, PUTROOTFH or PUTPUBFH set the current one, LOOKUP moves it, SAVEFH and RESTOREFH use the saved one as scratch space, and RENAME and LINK use both.

Evaluation stops at the first operation that returns a status other than NFS4_OK, and the results of everything evaluated so far are returned. There is no logical OR or AND of operations, and a COMPOUND is not a transaction: the client must recover from a partly completed request, so it should avoid overly complex ones. Operations that modify the file system are synchronous, so when one succeeds its data is in stable storage (the exception is a WRITE sent with the UNSTABLE4 option), and the server must not have the result of a later operation stored without the earlier ones.

The minorversion field is 0 for this RFC. A server that gets a minor version it does not support MUST return NFS4ERR_MINOR_VERS_MISMATCH.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of running to the shop three times for milk, bread and eggs, you hand over one shopping list. The shop works down the list and stops at the first thing it cannot find.

sections.title: RPC, Transport and Security
sections.content:
NFSv4 is an RPC application that uses RPC version 2 and XDR. The registered port 2049 SHOULD be the default, which means clients need not use the RPC binding protocols and the traffic can cross firewalls. Over IP, the transport MUST be an IETF-standardized transport that avoids network congestion, such as TCP or SCTP, and every implementation MUST support TCP. With TCP, clients and servers SHOULD use persistent connections.

Security uses the RPCSEC_GSS flavor, which MUST be implemented, although deploying it is optional. NFSv4 clients and servers MUST support the Kerberos V5 mechanism, with all three services: authentication only, integrity and privacy. Flavors such as AUTH_NONE, AUTH_SYS and AUTH_DH MAY also be implemented. The authentication model moves from the whole machine to the individual principal.

Because a server may offer several mechanisms at different points in its namespace, security is negotiated in band. A client starts with a minimal triple, and if the server answers NFS4ERR_WRONGSEC, the client uses the SECINFO operation to learn which triples are acceptable for that filehandle. The negotiation SHOULD itself happen over a secure channel. Callbacks from server to client MUST mutually authenticate, using the flavor of the original SETCLIENTID.

Retries are restricted. Over a reliable transport such as TCP the server MUST NOT silently drop a request unless the connection has broken, so a client MUST NOT retry unless the connection broke or the procedure is NULL. NULL is a recommended way to probe a connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you may enter the building, a guard checks a special badge. If the badge is not the right kind for a room, the guard tells you which kinds would work.

sections.title: Filehandles and Attributes
sections.content:
A filehandle is a per-server unique identifier for a file system object, and its contents are opaque to the client. NFSv4 drops the separate MOUNT protocol. Instead there are two special starting points: the root filehandle, reached with PUTROOTFH, and the public filehandle, reached with PUTPUBFH, whose binding is up to server policy. From the root the client walks the tree with LOOKUP.

Filehandles come in two kinds. A persistent filehandle stays fixed for the life of the object, even across server reboots or migration, and becomes stale only when the object is removed. A volatile filehandle may expire, and the server then answers NFS4ERR_FHEXPIRED. Clients learn which kind they have from the REQUIRED attribute fh_expire_type. A client with volatile handles should remember the component names leading to each object so it can look it up again.

Metadata is carried as attributes in three groups. REQUIRED attributes, such as type, size, change and fsid, must be supported by every client and server. RECOMMENDED attributes, such as acl, mode, owner and time_modify, may be absent, and a server should provide one only when it does not have to tell lies to the client. Named attributes are opaque byte streams reached through the OPENATTR operation, meant for application data. A client asks for attributes by setting bits in a GETATTR request, and can query which ones the server supports.

Access control uses the acl attribute, an array of access control entries that the server processes in order, with ALLOW and DENY entries deciding access and AUDIT and ALARM entries only triggering events. The mode attribute gives traditional UNIX-style permissions, and the RFC sets rules so the two stay consistent when either is set.
sections.plainLanguage: A filehandle is like the ticket number a coat check gives you: you do not need to know where your coat is hung, just show the ticket. Attributes are the little labels on the coat, like its size and who owns it.

sections.title: The Server Namespace and Multi-Server Namespaces
sections.content:
Servers usually share only parts of their file trees through exports. In NFSv2 and NFSv3 a client got each export's root through MOUNT and could not easily browse from one export to another. An NFSv4 server instead presents all its exports as one namespace, bridging the unexported gaps with a pseudo-file system: a read-only view of the exported directories only, with its own unique fsid. A client notices it has crossed into another file system when the fsid attribute changes. A server SHOULD NOT show a different namespace depending on the security mechanism in use, but return NFS4ERR_WRONGSEC for inappropriate access.

Namespaces can also span servers. The fs_locations attribute lists other places where a file system can be found, as a DNS name or literal IP address plus a path. A file system can be present at a position in the namespace, or absent: an absent file system holds no files or directories except the root, and almost any reference to it returns NFS4ERR_MOVED, except a GETATTR that asks for fs_locations. If a server ever returns NFS4ERR_MOVED, it MUST support fs_locations.

These mechanisms support three uses: replication (alternative copies to use if the current one becomes unavailable), migration (a file system moves to another server without disruption) and referrals (an absent file system that points the client at another server). Support is RECOMMENDED but use is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: The server shows you one big map of folders, even if they are stored in different rooms. If a folder has moved to another building, the map includes a note saying where to go.

sections.title: State, Locking and Leases
sections.content:
Putting byte-range locking and share reservations inside the protocol makes NFSv4 stateful. The server owns the state, and the client asks for changes. The old separate Network Lock Manager is replaced, and the design needs no callback for locking. A client first establishes identity with SETCLIENTID followed by SETCLIENTID_CONFIRM. It sends a verifier that changes on each client restart and a unique id string, and the server returns a 64-bit client ID. A new verifier tells the server the client rebooted, so it can drop the old state at once.

Each piece of state, whether an open, a set of byte-range locks, or a delegation, is named by a 128-bit stateid: a 96-bit other field plus a 32-bit seqid that rises with each change. Two special stateids exist: the anonymous stateid (all zeros) and the READ bypass stateid (all ones), used for I/O without open state. The OPEN operation combines lookup, creation and access checks, and carries a share reservation: the access wanted (read, write or both) and the access to deny others (none, read, write or both).

All state for a client hangs on one lease, a fixed interval set by the server (the lease_time attribute). Almost any operation with a valid client ID or stateid renews it, so renewal usually costs no extra RPCs, and in the worst case the RENEW operation is needed once per lease period. If a client crashes or is partitioned for longer than the lease, the server may free its locks.

If the server reboots, the client sees NFS4ERR_STALE_CLIENTID or NFS4ERR_STALE_STATEID and must get a new client ID. The server then runs a grace period at least as long as the previous lease, during which clients reclaim their locks and the server rejects ordinary lock requests and READ and WRITE operations with NFS4ERR_GRACE unless it can prove there is no conflict.
sections.plainLanguage: When you borrow a game console, the shop writes your name on a card and gives you a time limit. If you keep coming back to say hello, they keep your card. If you disappear for too long, they hand the console to someone else.

sections.title: Client-Side Caching and Delegations
sections.content:
NFSv4 does not provide distributed cache coherence. It defines a narrower set of caching guarantees so locks and share reservations are not disturbed by caching. Attributes and directory information are cached for a duration the client chooses, and file data validity is checked when a file is opened, with modified data written back at close.

The big addition is the delegation. When a file is opened, the server may hand the client a recallable delegation so the client can handle opens, closes and locks locally without asking the server. An OPEN_DELEGATE_READ delegation assures the client that no other client can write the file, and several can exist at once. An OPEN_DELEGATE_WRITE delegation assures that no other client reads or writes it, and only one can exist per file. The grant is the server's choice, so clients must never assume one will be given.

When another client makes a conflicting request, the server uses a callback (CB_RECALL) to recall the delegation. The holder must flush modified state and return it, and meanwhile the conflicting request waits or gets NFS4ERR_DELAY. A server grants delegations only after checking the callback path, using CB_NULL. If the client fails to respond, the server revokes the delegation, which makes any modified state still on the client useless. For a client with a write delegation, the server can fetch fresh file attributes with CB_GETATTR.
sections.plainLanguage: If nobody else wants the book you are reading, the librarian lets you keep it at your desk and stop checking in every time you turn a page. If someone else asks for it, you have to bring it back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Historically NFS treated the whole client machine, or its IP address, as the authenticated party, and AUTH_SYS simply named the user. The RFC calls this easy to deploy but not a safe model. NFSv4 therefore mandates support for end-to-end mutual authentication of an end user to a principal on the server, using cryptography that does not expose passwords or keys in the clear. Being required to implement does not mean required to use: AUTH_SYS can still be used, but interoperability through it is not assured.

Users may choose mechanisms without integrity protection for speed, which leaves them open to an attacker in the middle who modifies requests or replies. Two operations deserve protection regardless. SECINFO should be issued under a flavor with integrity, since otherwise an attacker could push the client toward a weaker choice. Any GETATTR for fs_locations SHOULD also use integrity protection, because an attacker could fake NFS4ERR_MOVED and then alter the reply to steer the client to a server the attacker controls.

SETCLIENTID and SETCLIENTID_CONFIRM release client state, so the server MUST NOT cancel a client's leased state if the principal issuing the request differs from the one that created it. Finally, UTF-8 file names and the owner and owner_group strings raise string-comparison issues, such as Unicode normalization. The strength of Kerberos V5 security depends on the existing Kerberos infrastructure, and the RFC points to RFC 6649 on why weak algorithms should be disabled by default.
sections.plainLanguage: Old NFS trusted anyone who walked in wearing the right company jacket. Version 4 checks each person's own ID card, and takes extra care when asking where things are stored, so nobody can send you to a fake address.

sections.title: Minor Versions, Names and IANA
sections.content:
NFSv4 is built to evolve. Each future minor version must be documented in a Standards Track RFC, and this RFC is minor version 0. Future minor versions extend rather than replace the XDR of the previous one, and new REQUIRED or RECOMMENDED attributes can be added by publishing a Standards Track RFC that allocates a number and defines the encoding.

File and directory names are encoded in UTF-8 to handle basic internationalization. Section 12 describes the behaviour of existing clients and servers, and its use of MUST, SHOULD and MAY reflects what implementations actually do rather than what is merely desirable.

The IANA section recaps the registry of named attribute definitions, which has no initial entries and uses the Specification Required policy. Names can be 1 to 128 UTF-8 characters, the prefix PRIV is for private use, and EXPE and STDS are reserved. Because this document obsoletes RFC 3530, IANA replaced references to RFC 3530 in two other registries.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule book says new chapters can be added later, as long as they are written down properly and the old chapters still work.
